newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore voters mull ruling party warnings, race.
newsitem.headline: Singapore voters mull ruling party warnings, race.

text.p: Singapore voters gave their verdicts on Thursday after a short but often bitter election campaign, where issues ranged from race to housing and healthcare.

State television reported queues before the 8.00 a.m. (0000 GMT) opening of polling stations in Jurong, where the battle for the West Coast multi-member constituency was between the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) and the Workers' Party (WP).

The toughest fight was expected in Cheng San constituency, which has become the focus of the latter part of the campaign in a bitter war of words between Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and WP candidate Tang Liang Hong over racial chauvinism.
Goh has said his personal prestige is at stake if Cheng San is lost. He was in the constituency for the poll opening.
One elderly voter leaving a polling station there told Reuters the fight would be tough: "Why else would the Prime Minister be coming to this centre?"

Opinion on the likely outcome at Cheng San was divided in talk at nearby coffee shops, but sentiment among many voters was that it was time for change and to see how the PAP would react if more opposition members were voted in.
Electors have been repeatedly told by Goh and leading ministers that upgrading of housing estates would not go ahead in constituencies that vote in opposition candidates.
Goh has said opposition estates would become slums.
One young restaurant manager was unperturbed by the threat. "I voted to live in a slum," he said after voting for an opposition candidate.
But a 60-year old Singaporean, who lives on a public housing estate, said he would still vote for the PAP, even though he did not like the government linking upgrading to voting.
"For all my grouses, I cannot cut off my nose to spite my face. I will vote for the PAP," he said.
A 27-year-old owner of two apartments who voted for the PAP said there was no reason to change a good thing. "I've done very well under the PAP."
The prosperity delivered to Singaporeans by the PAP was in evidence at a polling station in Chua Chu Kang where well-heeled voters arrived in Mercedes Benzes.

"For me the issue is not the upgrading. It is more the ministers' pay, the high-handedness of the government, the need for an alternative voice... essentially the soul of the people that I'm concerned about," said a property-owner who was voting for the opposition.
Protecting the vital spark of democracy was the motivation behind one 32-year old computer engineer's vote for the opposition at Aljunied constituency.
"The PAP needs to be kept in check," he said. "A single party leads to absolute power and this is unhealthy for democracy and Singapore."
